hook: The genius who invented calculus, binary numbers and a calculating machine.

pages.x: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz was born in Leipzig in 1646. His father, a professor, died when he was six, and the boy taught himself Latin from the books in his father's library. He went to university at 14 and had a doctorate in law at 20.
In 1673 he built a machine that could add, subtract, multiply and divide, using a stepped drum he invented.
pages.fx: His stepped drum was used in mechanical calculators for nearly 300 years, until electronic ones replaced them.

pages.x: In Paris around 1675 he worked out calculus, the mathematics of change, with the symbols still used today, like the long S of the integral.
pages.fx: Calculus became the language of physics, engineering and economics. Newton had found it first, but Leibniz published first, and his symbols won.

pages.x: A bitter quarrel broke out over who had invented calculus. The Royal Society, with Newton as its president, ruled that Leibniz had copied him; Newton secretly wrote the report himself. Historians now agree they found it separately.
He worked out binary arithmetic, writing every number with only 0 and 1, and was delighted to find it echoed in the ancient Chinese Book of Changes.
pages.fx: Binary is the language of every computer and phone today.

pages.t: The best of all possible worlds
pages.x: He argued that God had made this the best of all possible worlds. Half a century later the French writer Voltaire mocked the idea without mercy in his comic novel Candide.
He served the dukes of Hanover for 40 years, writing a history of their family that he never finished. When he died in 1716, hardly anyone came to his funeral.
Leibniz was one of the last people to master almost every field of knowledge. His calculus, his binary numbers and his philosophy still shape mathematics and computing.
pts: Invented calculus, at the same time as Newton
